title: US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850
summary: Start with where slavery was legal in late 1850 and the line Congress drew in 1820. Then turn on, one layer at a time, the routes along which enslaved people were sold south, two ships whose captives took control, and the routes people followed to escape.
subject: History
unit: Reform and the road to war
alsoFits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration
time: About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

image.alt: The map as it opens: the states and territories of late 1850, most of them named and each shaded in one of four blue or orange groups, with a dashed line running west from the bottom of Missouri.

map.about: This map shows the United States in late 1850, just after California became a state. Each state and territory is shaded in one of four groups, and a dashed line marks the Missouri Compromise line of 1820. Four more layers are off when the map opens: the routes of the slave trade within the United States, the routes of the ships La Amistad and Creole, and the approximate routes and cities of the Underground Railroad. Pop-ups give each area's group and the reason for it, and each route's direction.

(dark orange), territory open to slavery (light orange). The pop-up gives the group, the year a newer state was admitted and a one-sentence reason.

knownIssues.note: Outlines and routes come from two maps in an atlas printed in 1920: one of slavery and the slave trade in 1830 to 1850, and one of Underground Railroad routes in 1830 to 1865. They are approximate, and boundaries in the West are drawn as on those maps.

knownIssues.where: Free and slave states and territories, 1850
knownIssues.note: Texas is drawn with the boundary Congress set in the Compromise of 1850. The land it gave up north of the compromise line that was not put in New Mexico Territory appears as a separate area, "Unorganized land given up by Texas".

knownIssues.where: Routes of the slave trade within the United States; Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841)
knownIssues.note: The route lines have no arrowheads. The pop-up gives the direction people were moved.
The routes are approximate and carry no names, dates or other details; every route has the same pop-up.

The city pop-ups use today's abbreviations (for example WV for Morgantown and Parkersburg, which were in Virginia in 1850, NE for Nebraska City, and ON and QC for what were then Canada West and Canada East), and Rouses Point is listed under NH although it is in New York. Grinnell, Tabor and Nebraska City were founded after 1850, and Des Moines was a town of under 1,000 people in 1850, so the layer reflects the years up to the Civil War, not 1850 alone.

knownIssues.where: Free and slave states and territories, 1850 labels
knownIssues.note: Small eastern states may not be labeled at the national view. Clicking a state gives its name.

compellingQuestion.en: By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?

questions.task: With only the opening layers on, students read the legend, place a few states and territories in their groups, and find what New Jersey's pop-up adds to the word free.
frontOfClass: Open The United States in 1850 bookmark and open the legend.
Read the four groups aloud: free state, free territory, slave state (and Washington, D.C.), territory open to slavery.
Ask: where are the dark orange states, and where are the dark blue ones?
Click California, then Texas, and read the group and the year in each pop-up.
Click New Jersey. Ask: it is shaded as a free state. What does its pop-up add?

steps.en: Open The United States in 1850 bookmark and open the legend.
Click California, Texas, Oregon Territory and New Mexico Territory. Read the group at the top of each pop-up.
Click New Jersey and read the sentence under its group.

ask.en: (a) Which group is each of these in: California, Texas, Oregon Territory, New Mexico Territory? (b) In which part of the country are the slave states? (c) New Jersey is shaded as a free state. What does its pop-up say about people still held there in 1850?

answer.where: Free and slave states and territories, 1850 layer, legend and pop-ups. California: Free state (a state from 1850). Texas: Slave state (and Washington, D.C.) (a state from 1845); students can write slave state. Oregon Territory: Free territory. New Mexico Territory: Territory open to slavery. New Jersey: "An 1846 law abolished slavery here but kept the last enslaved people bound to their owners as 'apprentices'. The 1850 census still counted 236 people as enslaved."
answer.accept: (a) California free state; Texas slave state; Oregon Territory free territory; New Mexico Territory open to slavery. (b) The South and Southeast, from Delaware and Maryland down to Florida and west to Texas, plus Missouri. (c) The census of 1850 still counted 236 people as enslaved there, bound to their owners as "apprentices", so a free state was not free for everyone.
answer.text: The layer has 16 free states and 15 slave states, plus the District of Columbia. The counts are hard to make at the national view because the small eastern states are tiny and mostly unlabeled, so the question asks for groups and examples instead.

questions.task: Students read the dashed line's pop-up, then find one place that breaks its rule on each side of the year 1850: Missouri, and Utah Territory.
frontOfClass: Click the dashed line and read its year and description.
Ask: north of this line, what was supposed to be true?
Click Missouri and read the note. Ask: which side of the line is most of Missouri on, and which group is it in?
Click Unorganized territory, then Utah Territory. Ask: both are north of the line's latitude. Why are they in different groups?
Point out where the dashed line stops in the west.

steps.en: Click the dashed line. Read the year and the description.
Click Missouri, the orange state just north of the east end of the dashed line (its name may not show). Read the sentence in its pop-up about the line.
Click Unorganized territory and then Utah Territory. Read the reason in each pop-up.
Look at where the dashed line ends in the west.

ask.en: (a) What did the line of 1820 decide? (b) How is Missouri an exception to it? (c) Unorganized territory and Utah Territory are both north of the line's latitude. Which law decided about slavery in each one, and what did it say?

answer.where: Missouri Compromise line pop-up: "Enacted 1820"; 36°30′ north was the northern limit of slavery in the Louisiana Territory, except Missouri, admitted as a slave state, with Maine admitted as a free state. Missouri pop-up: admitted under the Missouri Compromise of 1820, "although almost all of it lies north of the compromise line". Unorganized territory: "Closed to slavery by the Missouri Compromise of 1820, because it lies north of the compromise line." Utah Territory: "Organized by the Compromise of 1850, which left slavery for the settlers to decide."
answer.accept: (a) Slavery was not allowed north of 36°30′ in the Louisiana Territory, except in Missouri; Maine came in as a free state to keep the balance. (b) Almost all of Missouri is north of the line, but it is a slave state. (c) Unorganized territory: the Missouri Compromise of 1820 closed it to slavery. Utah Territory: the Compromise of 1850 left slavery for its settlers to decide. Strong answers notice that the dashed line stops at the edge of New Mexico Territory and is not drawn across the land organized in 1850.
answer.text: The law of 1820 applied to the land of the Louisiana Purchase. Almost all of Utah and New Mexico Territories came from land Mexico gave up in 1848; eastern New Mexico had also been claimed by Texas until 1850, and Utah's pop-up notes a small area on its eastern edge that was not part of that land. Instead of extending the line of 1820, Congress wrote a different rule for the two new territories. Students don't need this to answer from the map; it explains why the dashed line stops at the edge of New Mexico Territory.

questions.task: Before any route layer is on, students write down where they think enslaved people were being sold from and to inside the United States, and why.
frontOfClass: Open The South bookmark. Keep the route layers off.
Say: inside the slave states, enslaved people were sold and moved from one region to another.
Ask: from which part of the orange states, and toward which part? What makes you think so? Have students write it down before any layer is turned on.

steps.en: Open The South bookmark. Leave the other layers off.
Write your idea down before you turn anything on.

ask.en: Inside the slave states, enslaved people were sold from one region to another. Which way do you think most of them were moved, and what makes you think so?

fill.en: I think most were moved from ______________ toward ______________ because ______________.

answer.accept: Any direction with a reason, for example toward newer states where land was being cleared for cotton, or toward ports. The idea is tested in question 4, so it is not marked right or wrong here.

questions.task: Students turn on the slave trade routes, read the direction and account for the land and sea routes, and compare what they see with what they wrote in question 3.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Routes of the slave trade within the United States.
Open The South bookmark.
Click a black line on land and read Direction people were moved and the account under it.
Click a black line at sea and do the same.
Ask: the lines have no arrows. Where do they start, where do many of them meet, and how do you know which way people were moved?
Ask: how does this compare with what you wrote in question 3?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Routes of the slave trade within the United States.
Open The South bookmark.
Click a black line on land. Read Direction people were moved and the account under it.
Click a black line at sea and read its pop-up too.

ask.en: (a) In which direction were enslaved people moved, by land and by sea? (b) Name two states the pop-up gives as places people were taken from, and the kind of country they were taken to. (c) Near which city or state do many of the lines meet? (d) Was your idea in question 3 right?

answer.where: Routes of the slave trade within the United States layer and pop-ups. Overland routes: direction "South and west"; "from the Upper South, such as Virginia and Maryland, to the cotton and sugar country of the Deep South". Sea routes: "South and west, by sea"; "along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from ports in the Upper South toward New Orleans". On the map many land and sea lines meet at New Orleans, in Louisiana.
answer.accept: (a) South and west. (b) From Virginia and Maryland (the Upper South) to the cotton and sugar country of the Deep South. (c) New Orleans, in Louisiana (accept Louisiana, or the mouth of the Mississippi River). (d) Any honest comparison with the earlier idea.
answer.text: The lines have no arrowheads, so the pop-up is the evidence for direction. Almost all of these routes lie inside the slave states or off their coasts. One follows the Ohio River, the border between slave states and free states; the map draws it a little north of the river, so it appears to cross the southern edge of Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. Federal law allowed this trade between the slave states in 1850. The Compromise of 1850 restricted it in one place: from January 1, 1851, nobody could bring enslaved people into Washington, D.C., to sell them.

questions.task: Students turn on the two ship routes and compare where each voyage ended and what happened to the people on board.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841).
Open The United States in 1850 bookmark.
Click the dashed line that runs up the Atlantic coast and read its pop-up.
Click the shorter dashed line and read its pop-up.
Ask: where did each voyage end, and who decided what happened to the people on board?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn off Routes of the slave trade within the United States and turn on Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841).
Open The United States in 1850 bookmark.
Click each of the two dashed lines at sea and read its pop-up.

ask.en: (a) Where did La Amistad start, and where did it end up? (b) Where was the Creole going, and where did the people on board take it instead? (c) What happened to the people on each ship in the end?

answer.where: Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841) layer and pop-ups. La Amistad, 1839: from Cuba north to Long Island, New York; Africans who had been enslaved illegally took over the ship; in 1841 the Supreme Court ruled that they were free. Creole, 1841: enslaved people being shipped from Virginia to New Orleans took over the ship and sailed it to Nassau, in the British Bahamas, where most of them were freed.
answer.accept: (a) It started off Cuba and reached Long Island, New York. (b) It was going from Virginia to New Orleans; the people on board took it to Nassau, in the Bahamas. (c) The Supreme Court ruled in 1841 that the Africans from La Amistad were free; most of the people on the Creole were freed in the British Bahamas.
answer.text: The Creole was sailing one of the sea routes students saw in question 4. Britain had ended slavery in its colonies in the 1830s, which is why reaching Nassau mattered.

questions.task: Students swap the trade routes for the Underground Railroad layers, follow the routes north, find the cities in Canada and measure how far beyond the Ohio River one route runs.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn off Routes of the slave trade within the United States and Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841). Turn on Underground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities.
Open The Ohio River and the North bookmark.
Ask: which way do the green lines run, compared with the black lines in question 4?
Click dots near the top of the map until you find a city in Canada.
Use Measure to draw a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, on the Ohio River, to Chatham, in Canada. Chatham is the dot just east of Detroit; click it to check.
Ask: Ohio was a free state. Why might a route keep going this far past it?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn off the two route layers from questions 4 and 5. Turn on Underground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities.
Open The Ohio River and the North bookmark.
Click the dots on the unshaded land north of the blue states. They lie north of the Great Lakes and along the St. Lawrence River. Read the country in each pop-up.
Use Measure to draw a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, in Canada. Chatham is the dot just east of Detroit; click it to check.

ask.en: (a) Which way do these routes run, compared with the slave trade routes? (b) Name the three cities in Canada. (c) About how far is it in a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, Canada? (d) Ohio was a free state. What does that distance suggest about how safe a free state was for someone who had escaped?

fill.en: Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, Canada: about ________ miles

answer.where: Underground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities layers. The green lines run north and northeast from the slave states to the Great Lakes, New England and Canada, the opposite of the trade routes. Cities in Canada: Chatham and Toronto (ON) and Montreal (QC). Measure, Ripley to Chatham: about 265 miles in a straight line (accept 240 to 290). The green lines reach Montreal and the Detroit River and cross Lake Erie; they stop short of the Chatham and Toronto dots.
answer.accept: (a) North, the opposite way. (b) Chatham, Toronto and Montreal. (c) About 265 miles. (d) People kept going hundreds of miles past the free states to Canada, which suggests they were not safe from capture in a free state.
answer.text: The reason is not on the map. The Constitution and a law of 1793 already let slaveholders reclaim people who had escaped to free states. The Fugitive Slave Act of September 1850, part of the Compromise of 1850, made that much easier to enforce: federal commissioners heard the claims, the person claimed could not testify, citizens could be ordered to help, and anyone who helped a person escape could be fined and jailed. Ohio has more named cities on these routes than any other state (14 of the 69).

questions.task: Students read what the Underground Railroad pop-up says about its own routes and consider what a map drawn from an atlas of 1920 can and can't show.
frontOfClass: Click any Underground Railroad route (a thin green line) and read its pop-up.
Ask: why are these routes only approximate?
Ask: the map shows where routes ran. What does it not tell you about the people who were moved along them, or who escaped?

steps.en: Click any Underground Railroad route (a thin green line) and read its pop-up.
Think about what you could count or name on this map, and what you could not.

ask.en: (a) Why does the pop-up call these routes approximate? (b) Name one thing about the people on these routes that the map does not show. (c) What other kind of source would help you find it out?

answer.where: Underground Railroad approximate routes pop-up: "An approximate route that people escaping slavery followed north. The Underground Railroad was secret, so no exact routes were recorded." The trade route pop-ups add: "The line is approximate, from a 1920 atlas map."
answer.accept: (a) The Underground Railroad was secret, so nobody recorded exact routes. (b) For example their names, how many people there were, what happened to them, or what the journey was like. (c) For example narratives written by people who escaped, letters, newspapers, ship or sale records, or census counts.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least three layers and two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. Accept answers that describe the division on the map (free states in the North and California, free territories in the North and Northwest, slave states in the South, and Utah, New Mexico and Indian Territory open to slavery, with the line of 1820 and the exceptions of Missouri and Utah Territory) and say what it meant for enslaved people: being sold south and west along the trade routes, and escaping north, in many cases as far as Canada. Strong answers use New Jersey or the distance to Canada to show that free did not mean safe.

student.en: Answer the big question, By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?, with evidence from at least three layers and two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map leaves you with.

objectives: Use the legend and pop-ups to place states and territories of late 1850 in four groups, and read the reason given for each.
Explain what the Missouri Compromise line decided, and how Missouri and Utah Territory differ from its rule.
Test an idea about the direction of the slave trade within the United States against the routes and their pop-ups.
Follow the routes of La Amistad, the Creole and the Underground Railroad, and use a measured distance as evidence about safety in free states.
Say what a map drawn from a 1920 atlas can and can't show about the people on these routes.
discussion: In question 3 you wrote where you thought enslaved people were moved. What was your idea based on, and what did the routes change?
The trade routes run south and west and the escape routes run north. What does putting the two on one map show that either one alone would not?
Two territories in 1850 were left for settlers to decide. What might follow from leaving that question open?

differentiation.support: Questions 1 and 2 work well from the front with the legend open; pairs can then take one route layer each in questions 4 to 6 and report what the pop-ups say.
differentiation.stretch: With Measure, compare the Creole's planned voyage from Virginia to New Orleans along the sea route with the distance it sailed to Nassau, and suggest why the people on board chose Nassau.

resources.title: Avenues of Escape on the Underground Railroad

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the four groups and the line of 1820, an exception (Missouri, Utah Territory or New Jersey's 236 people), the direction of the trade routes toward New Orleans, and the escape routes north to Canada (Chatham, Toronto and Montreal are marked), with the measured distance.
assessment.exemplar: By 1850 slavery split the country into two parts. On the map the free states are in the North and the slave states are in the South, and a dashed line from 1820 was supposed to keep slavery out of the land north of it. It did not settle things, because Missouri is a slave state north of the line, and Utah Territory was left for its settlers to decide. For enslaved people the split meant being moved against their will. The black routes go south and west, from Virginia and Maryland to the cotton and sugar country, and many of them meet at New Orleans. The green routes go the other way, north to Canada, where the map marks Chatham, Toronto and Montreal. Chatham is about 265 miles past the Ohio River, so crossing into a free state was not enough to be safe. Even New Jersey, a free state, still counted 236 people as enslaved.

beforeYouStart.en: In 1850 slavery was legal in some states and banned in others. A territory was land that belonged to the United States but was not yet a state. Twice, in 1820 and in 1850, Congress passed a compromise, an agreement where each side gives something up, about where slavery would be allowed. People who were enslaved were bought and sold, and many were forced to move far from their families. Some escaped. This map is traced from an atlas printed in 1920.

readingTheMap.en: Dark blue: free state. Light blue: free territory. Dark orange: slave state, and Washington, D.C. Light orange: territory open to slavery. The dashed gray line is the Missouri Compromise line. Only these two layers are on at the start; turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. Solid black lines are slave trade routes. The two dashed lines at sea are two ships. The thinner green lines and the black dots are the Underground Railroad. The legend names each one. No line has arrows: click it and the pop-up gives the direction. Small states may have no name on the map; click one to see it.

reflection.en: Which layer changed your picture of 1850 the most when you turned it on, and what did it add?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The map opens with only the states and territories and the Missouri Compromise line on. Students turn on the slave trade routes in question 4, the two ships in question 5 and the Underground Railroad layers in question 6, where the earlier route layers go off so the green lines stand out. Question 3's idea is best written down before any route layer is on. The subject is the buying, selling and forced movement of people, and some students may have family histories connected to it; the questions ask what the map shows and avoid asking students to imagine themselves enslaved or to defend slavery. The pop-ups use the terms enslaved people and people escaping slavery. Question 6 uses Measure; a straight line from Ripley to Chatham is enough.

misconceptions.claim: A free state had no enslaved people.
misconceptions.response: New Jersey's pop-up says the 1850 census still counted 236 people as enslaved there.

misconceptions.claim: The Missouri Compromise line settled where slavery could go.
misconceptions.response: Missouri is a slave state north of the line, and in 1850 Utah and New Mexico Territories were left for their settlers to decide.

misconceptions.claim: People who escaped were safe once they reached a free state.
misconceptions.response: The routes on the map continue through the free states to Canada, where the cities layer marks Chatham, Toronto and Montreal.

misconceptions.claim: The Underground Railroad was a real railroad with fixed tracks.
misconceptions.response: The pop-up calls the routes approximate: it was a secret network of people and places, and no exact routes were recorded.

standards.text: Analyze the role of slavery in the development of sectional conflict
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
